subject: business-studies
title: The BCG Matrix
welcome_lead: Stars, Cows, Question Marks, Dogs - a portfolio in four boxes.
meta_desc: A-Level BCG: four quadrants of the Boston matrix.
final_note: Use BCG to balance cash flow today against growth tomorrow.

concepts.def: High share, high growth - invest to defend leadership.
High share, low growth - milk for cash.
Low share, high growth - invest or divest.
Low share, low growth - usually divest.
Firm's share divided by largest rival's share.
Annual percentage growth in market sales.

walkthroughs.body_html: Plot each product on relative market share (horizontal, log scale) and market growth (vertical). The four quadrants suggest the cash position and strategy for each product.
Cash cows fund stars and question marks. Dogs leak cash. Question marks need decisive action - back the winners, drop the rest.
BCG assumes share drives cost via experience curves. In differentiated markets a niche dog can be very profitable. BCG is a portfolio aid, not a destiny.

mcqs.q: A high-share product in a low-growth market is a:
options: Star
Cash Cow
Question Mark
Dog

mcqs.q: Cash from cows is typically used to fund:
options: Dogs only
Stars and question marks
Share buybacks only
Dividends only

mcqs.q: What four growth strategies does Ansoff's Matrix identify?
options: Ansoff's Matrix shows market share against profit.

Market penetration (existing product, existing market), market development (existing product, new market), product development (new product, existing market), diversification (new product, new market).
Ansoff's Matrix is about analysing competitors.
Profitable businesses fail only when employees steal.

mcqs.q: Why does a company's share price change?
options: Profitable businesses fail only when employees steal.
Share prices go up when a company makes more money this year.
Share prices are set by the government each morning.
Share prices reflect investors' expectations about future profits — driven by company performance, sector trends, economic conditions, and market sentiment.

mcqs.q: Why can a profitable business still fail?
options: If a business is profitable it cannot run out of money.
Profitable businesses fail only when employees steal.
Ansoff's Matrix shows market share against profit.
Because cash flow and profit are different — a business may be profitable on paper but run out of cash to pay bills, especially if customers owe money or stock ties up funds.
